newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK economy steams ahead with handover on horizon.
newsitem.headline: HK economy steams ahead with handover on horizon.

text.p: Hong Kong unveiled an impressive set of first quarter economic numbers on Friday, confirming rising consumer confidence before the territory's return to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.

Just as the Hang Seng stock index soared to close at a fresh record high, the Hong Kong government disclosed a sturdy economy that grew at a "somewhat faster" clip than the 5.5-percent rate notched up in the first quarter.
"The pick-up in economic activity during the course of 1996 was generally sustained into the first quarter of 1997," the government said in its first quarter economic report.
Consumer spending remained the driving force, even while inflation showed signs of moderation.
Bullish sentiment in the property market prevailed throughout the period. Retail sales grew 1.9 percent while sales of consumer durables rose 11.3 percent.

"There was a strong demand for higher-value items and consumer durables, including particularly motor vehicles. There were also signs that business at restaurants was turning better," the government said.
Inflation steadied despite the optimism, which was best reflected by Friday's 341-point gain in the Hang Seng index to a fresh record high close of 14,757.81.

The benchmark consumer price index (A) rose by 6.2 percent in the first quarter compared to 6.0 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, while the composite CPI -- a blend of three separate consumer price indices -- remained flat at 6.1 percent.
"There was nevertheless some deceleration in inflation within the first quarter of 1997," the government said.

However, the GDP deflator, a broad measure of overall inflation in the economy, rose 6.2 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, "appreciably faster" than the 5.2 percent increase in the first half of last year.
The external sector struck the only bleak note.

While the domestic economy beamed out positive signals, exports continued to lag in the first quarter, reflecting the sluggish turnaround throughout the region following last year's sudden collapse in Asian exports.
Hong Kong's total exports rose two percent, while re-exports -- goods shipped through the territory for processing elsewhere -- rose four percent. Domestic exports sank six percent.
Several factors were responsible for the disappointing showing, the government said.

The relative strength of the U.S. dollar continued to weaken the competitiveness of Hong Kong's exports overseas, while the dispute between Hong Kong and the United States over alleged quota abuse for textiles and clothing exports to the United States could have curtailed orders.
"Moreover, the global oversupply of electronic products had dampened Hong Kong's exports of such products since the early part of 1996," the government said.
